reading.body:
The exam rarely asks a rate's number. It asks who sets the rate and which one is lowest or most volatile. Learn the four named rates.

**Fed funds rate** is the overnight rate banks charge each other on reserves. The FOMC sets a target range. It is the **most volatile** rate because the market sets it daily.

**Discount rate** is what the **Fed** charges banks that borrow at the discount window. The Fed Board sets it.

**Prime rate** is what banks charge their best corporate customers. **Banks** set it.

**Broker call rate** is what banks charge broker-dealers on margin funding.

Rank them lowest to highest: **fed funds < discount < broker call < prime.**

reading.h: Inflation, deflation, and the real rate
reading.body:
**Inflation** is a general rise in prices and a fall in purchasing power. The **CPI** measures it, and so do PPI and PCE. **Deflation** is falling prices. **Stagflation** is inflation plus a stagnant economy.

Rising inflation pushes the Fed to tighten. Rates rise, so bond prices fall. Inflation hurts fixed-payment assets most: bonds, preferred stock, and fixed annuities. It helps real assets: real estate, commodities, and TIPS.

The **real rate = nominal rate − inflation**. A 5% bond during 3% inflation gives about a **2%** real return.

reading.h: GDP, the business cycle, and sectors
reading.body:
**GDP** is the value of everything produced **inside** the country. **GNP** is everything produced by the country's **nationals** wherever they are. The textbook **recession** is **two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP**.

The business cycle runs **expansion → peak → contraction → trough → recovery**.

Sectors behave differently. **Cyclical** stocks (autos, housing, steel, luxury) move **with** the cycle. **Defensive** stocks (utilities, food, pharma, tobacco) resist downturns because people buy their products in any economy. **Growth** stocks beat the market in expansions. **Counter-cyclical** assets like gold can move the opposite way.

**Leading** indicators turn **before** the economy: stock prices (S&P 500), building permits, **initial jobless claims**, money supply (M2), new orders, average weekly manufacturing hours, and the yield spread.

**Coincident** indicators turn **with** the economy: GDP, industrial production, personal income, and nonfarm payrolls.

**Lagging** indicators turn **after** the economy: the **unemployment rate**, CPI, prime rate, average duration of unemployment, and business inventories.

The exam's favorite trap: jobless **claims** lead, but the unemployment **rate** and the duration of unemployment lag. Stock prices lead.

reading.h: Monetary vs fiscal policy — and the one causal chain
reading.body:
**Monetary policy** is the **Fed's** job. Its main tool is **open-market operations** by the FOMC. When the Fed **buys** Treasuries it adds reserves (easy money). Rates fall, **bond prices rise**, stocks usually rise, and the dollar weakens. When the Fed **sells**, it drains reserves (tight money) and the chain reverses.

Other tools are the **discount rate**, the **reserve requirement**, and IORB. The reserve requirement has been **0% since 2020**, but the exam still calls it the most powerful, least used tool.

**Fiscal policy** is **Congress and the President's** job: taxes and government spending. The schools of thought are **Keynesian** (manage demand with fiscal policy), **monetarist / Friedman** (steady money-supply growth), and **supply-side** (cut taxes and regulation).

reading.h: Yield curve, the dollar, indexes, and circuit breakers
reading.body:
The **yield curve** plots Treasury yields by maturity. A **normal (positive)** curve slopes up, with long rates higher than short rates, and signals expansion. An **inverted** curve has short rates above long rates and has historically come before recessions.

A **strong dollar** makes imports cheap and U.S. exports expensive. It hurts exporters and helps importers and tourists abroad. A weak dollar does the reverse.

For indexes, the DJIA holds 30 stocks and is **price-weighted**. The **S&P 500** is cap-weighted and is the benchmark for market-wide **circuit breakers**. An S&P 500 drop of **7% (Level 1)** or **13% (Level 2)** before 3:25 pm triggers a 15-minute halt. A **20% (Level 3)** drop at any time closes the market for the day.

flashcards.back: Fed funds < discount < broker call < prime. Fed funds is the most volatile.

flashcards.front: Which named rate does the Fed set directly?
flashcards.back: The discount rate (Fed Board). Fed funds is targeted but set by the market; banks set prime and broker call.
Nominal rate − inflation. A 5% bond in 3% inflation = about 2% real.
GDP = produced inside the country; GNP = produced by the country's nationals anywhere. Recession = two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP.
Cyclical (autos, housing, steel, luxury) move with the cycle; defensive (utilities, food, pharma, tobacco) resist downturns.

flashcards.front: Leading vs coincident vs lagging: the classic trap
flashcards.back: Jobless CLAIMS and stock prices LEAD; the unemployment RATE and duration of unemployment LAG; GDP is coincident.
Reserves up → money supply up → rates down → bond prices up → stocks up → dollar weaker. (Selling reverses it.)
0% since 2020 — but the exam still calls it the most powerful, least used Fed tool.

flashcards.front: Monetary vs fiscal policy — who runs each?
flashcards.back: Monetary = the Fed (open-market ops, discount rate, reserves). Fiscal = Congress + President (taxes and spending).
Short-term rates above long-term rates; has historically come before a recession.
DJIA = 30 stocks, price-weighted. S&P 500 = cap-weighted; the circuit-breaker benchmark.

quiz.stem: Your savings account pays 2% a year. Over the same year, the prices of the things you buy rise by 3%. What happens to what your savings can buy?
options: It grows, because the balance is larger than a year ago
It shrinks, because prices rose faster than the balance grew
It stays the same, because the interest offsets the price increases
It shrinks by exactly 3%, because interest does not count against inflation
quiz.explanation: Real return = nominal rate − inflation = 2% − 3% ≈ −1%, so purchasing power falls even though the dollar balance rose. The interest does count; it just does not fully offset the 3% price rise.

quiz.stem: The Federal Open Market Committee directs the SALE of Treasury securities in the open market. Which of the following is the MOST likely result?
options: Bank reserves increase and short-term interest rates fall
The money supply expands and bond prices rise
Bank reserves increase and bond prices fall
The money supply contracts and bond prices fall
quiz.explanation: When the Fed sells securities it drains reserves from the banking system (tight money): money supply down, interest rates up, and therefore bond prices down. Buying securities produces the opposite chain.

quiz.stem: All of the following are considered leading economic indicators EXCEPT:
options: Average weekly initial claims for unemployment insurance
New building permits for private housing
Stock prices as measured by the S&P 500
Average duration of unemployment
quiz.explanation: Initial jobless claims, building permits, and stock prices all turn before the economy and are leading indicators; the average duration of unemployment is a lagging indicator. The trap is that jobless claims lead while measures of the unemployment situation lag.

quiz.stem: Which of the following interest rates is set directly by the Federal Reserve rather than by banks or the market?
options: The federal funds rate
The discount rate
The prime rate
The broker call loan rate
quiz.explanation: The Fed Board sets the discount rate it charges banks at the discount window. The fed funds rate is charged bank-to-bank and moves within a target range the FOMC sets (targeted, not set), while prime and broker call rates are set by commercial banks.

quiz.stem: The Federal Reserve BUYS Treasury securities on the open market. All of the following are likely effects EXCEPT:
options: Bank reserves increase
Short-term interest rates fall
Bond prices rise
The money supply contracts
quiz.explanation: Buying securities adds reserves and EXPANDS the money supply (easy money), pushing rates down and bond prices up. A contracting money supply is the result of the Fed selling securities, not buying — so that is the exception.

quiz.stem: During an economic contraction, which sector's stocks would an analyst expect to hold up BEST?
options: Automobile manufacturers
Home builders
Electric utilities and food producers
Luxury-goods retailers
quiz.explanation: Defensive sectors — utilities, food, pharma, tobacco — sell products people buy in any economy, so they resist downturns. Autos, housing, and luxury goods are cyclical and fall with the economy.

quiz.stem: By the textbook definition, an economy is in a recession when:
options: The stock market falls by 20% or more
Real GDP declines for two consecutive quarters
The unemployment rate rises for one month
The yield curve inverts
quiz.explanation: The textbook recession is two consecutive quarters of declining real GDP. A 20% market drop, a one-month rise in unemployment, or an inverted yield curve may accompany or precede a recession but are not its definition.
